picks.reasoning: Stubborn and blunt: GEN have better hands in more roles than IG. Chovy and Ruler give them a steady mid-bot axis, and the jungle and bot play is what builds early tempo, so I'm not leaning on Chovy over Rookie alone. The LCK-over-LPL gap is real and I'm leaning on it hard. Rookie can still steal a game with a comfort pick and Wei's jungle pressure, so I'm giving IG one, but I'm not hedging to a fifth game. I only flip if Rookie wins mid and Wei takes jungle control in the first fifteen minutes across multiple games.

usedLessons.text: Top lesson: One win doesn't prove my Chovy-over-Rookie call, because the debate showed GEN took early tempo and the map, not that Chovy won lane. Next time I'll back the side whose players are stronger across several roles, especially jungle and bot, since that's what builds early tempo, and not lean on a single marquee lane. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but under Fearless drafts that skill includes champion pool depth, so I should check whether the star players can keep finding strong picks game after game before I trust them to win clean. A flagged big region gap is a reason to back the better players, not a reason to ignore the one opposing player (like Isles) who can steal a game, so I'll keep my confidence moderate and my scoreline honest. (from Swiss LYON vs IG; picked IG 2-1, actual IG 2-1)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, and Chovy and Ruler's steadiness beating Zeka's flash backs that up, so I should keep backing the stronger players and not let an early-game hype story like HLE's aggression make me flinch. One win doesn't make me right about everything, though: when I name a risk like a Zeka lane win, I should state exactly which player matchup would have to break before I change my pick, since that's where skill actually decides the game. (from Swiss GEN vs HLE; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Top lesson: When I back the stronger players, I should trust them to close games rather than hedge toward a fifth game out of fear of one opponent's comfort picks, because individual skill shows up as tempo, and early leads are where it turns into wins. I still won't let crowd hype or team-stat samples pull me off the better hands, but I'll check whether those hands have actually been winning the first fifteen minutes before I price in a scramble. (from Quarterfinals TES vs IG; picked IG 3-2, actual IG 3-1)

usedLessons.text: Jungle lesson: The early game still decides everything, so when a big region gap is flagged, I should confirm it shows up as first-15-minute tempo (jungle pathing, lane priority, first objectives) and not lean on star names or records. I can also borrow Mid's draft point: a deep draft is what hands you that early priority, so I'll check whether a team's picks set up the first tower and dragon before I raise my confidence. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Jungle lesson: GEN won because Canyon owned the first 15 minutes (the Herald and dragon tempo I flagged), so when a team with a proven jungle edge faces an early-aggro opponent, I should trust the tempo matchup and lean harder instead of hedging at 57. HLE's blood-in-the-first-five setups only matter if they convert into objectives, so next time I'll check whether they've actually turned early kills into Herald and towers against this opponent before fearing the snowball. Jungle lesson: When one side keeps winning the first 15 minutes (Herald, plates, first dragon) and the report flags a big region gap, I shouldn't hand the underdog a game just because a jungler's pathing could steal one. Fearless drafts don't undo a tempo edge that big, so I'll only pick the upset if I can point to a real early-game trigger already showing up for them, not just a flip condition on paper. (from Swiss G2 vs HLE; picked HLE 2-1, actual HLE 2-0)

Jungle lesson: Early tempo decided this one, as it always does, so I'll keep asking who actually took first blood, first tower and the early map against top-tier opposition, and I'll discount early-game numbers that were built against weaker competition. I'll also keep naming concrete flip triggers like first Drake and Herald, because tempo shows up in the objective timeline and not in the hype. (from Swiss TSW vs IG; picked IG, actual IG 1-0)

usedLessons.text: Mid lesson: Fearless depth still decides series, but I should show it through specific draft outcomes, like which jungle and lane picks give GEN early tempo and priority, rather than a general "more answers" claim. I also shouldn't lean on a league-gap argument or domestic records unless the scouting report flags a BIG REGION GAP, because the draft and the star's pool are the real case. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Mid lesson: Fearless pool depth only matters if it shows up in the early draft, so next time I should check which side actually gets lane and jungle priority from the first picks (like IG's Wei tempo) before treating a flexible star like Rookie as a reason for a close series. When the star's flex pool and the jungle tempo point the same way, I should lean toward the faster series, 3-1 rather than 3-2, instead of hedging on a comeback draft that the opponent may never get to play. Mid lesson: A correct 2-1 doesn't prove my draft read, so next time I'll name the Fearless picks that should decide each game (Rookie's pool, Wei's tempo picks, LYON's comfort picks) and grade myself on whether those drafts actually happened, not just the scoreline. Pool depth matters most by game three, when the best champions are locked out, so I'll check who still has comfortable picks left instead of leaning on a vague tiebreaker. Mid lesson: Draft decides a Bo1, but the draft read only counts if I name the specific failure condition (HLE's early-priority pick into a first-rotation fight) and check it against how the picks and the lanes actually played out, not just credit Chovy's comfort pool after the win. Next time I'll weigh how much each team's draft can stay flexible under bans and Fearless restrictions, so a lopsided H2H history stays a tiebreaker and never becomes the reason I lean on a side. (from Swiss GEN vs HLE; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

usedLessons.text: ADC lesson: When the head-to-head is dead even (3-3), a bigger domestic series-wins total is only a weak tiebreaker.
